utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Good afternoon, Your Honours. Case Number IT-99-36-T, The Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Mr. Brdjanin, good afternoon to you. Can you follow in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. Appearances, Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Joanna Korner, Ann Sutherland, assisted by Denise Gustin, case manager. Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you. Appearances for Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. I'm John Ackerman appearing with David Cunningham and Aleksandar Vujic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you and good afternoon to you all. I understand there are some preliminaries.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just two really administrative matters Your Honour. The first relates to sitting dates. We have been told that the holiday has changed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I got notice of it today which basically means that we will have to change -- before it was the 26th, now it's the 25th. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's -- see, I haven't had time honestly today to --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I leave that with Your Honours to consider.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, I have it on my desk, a note on my desk to find out exactly what we should do next, how to go about this. But obviously what it entails is we were not sitting on the 26th, now we will be sitting on the 26th. And we were sitting on the 25th, and we will not sit on the 25th. So when -- that week are we sitting in the morning or the afternoon? That's when we were supposed to resume on the 25th.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We were supposed to resume on Tuesday the 25th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And now we won't be able to resume on Tuesday the 25th.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Not likely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we will resume on the 26th.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour is not suggesting we sit on Monday the 24th --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I am available.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I see Mr. Ackerman arranged -- he's shaking his head. We'll start on the Wednesday, then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. It doesn't make any difference because we were starting and stopping Wednesday --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We lose one more day, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It doesn't make a difference.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Quite right. Your Honour, the other thing I understand has changed which is the plenary which is no longer the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The 12th.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It was the 17th and 18th or something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, the week before.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's confirmed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: To my knowledge. But I haven't got an indication that the dates have changed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: They have been fixed quite some time ago, and unusually a week before --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But that's the position.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Thank you, Your Honour. And finally, this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That should be one day.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That is one day, is it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Probably. Probably. Probably one.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then finally Your Honour, in relation to the judgement, the written judgement, can I just raise it for this reason: We got information that Banja Luka Radio reported that Mr. Brdjanin had been -- that your ruling had dismissed all the charges of genocide as well as those related to count -- the count relating to destruction of cultural and religious heritage. Your Honour, we all know these things happen but we think it would assist if Your Honours were able to tell us when we're likely to get the written document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's being finalised. It's the very end of the exercise.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. But unfortunately I had my main legal officer in charge this week who was sick, and plus I was involved in sittings in the morning and the afternoon the whole week.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I perhaps make it clear to dispel any illusions that Banja Luka may be under, that Your Honours' rulings did not dismiss the discharges of genocide or the charges of destruction of cultural and religious heritage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Actually, Ms. Korner, it makes me feel at home because I spent 25 years of my career as a Judge reading reports of my own judgements which I never gave.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So believe me, I suppose that is enough. I don't blame anyone because sometimes reporters are not up to the standard that one would expect. But -- and sometimes our decisions are not easy to comprehend as well. But to make it clear, I mean, if the Banja Luka paper or media reported what my -- our oral decision the way you put it, then they are --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In error.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Very much so. Very much so.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. That's all I want to raise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman. You wrote the article in the Banja Luka --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I didn't, Your Honour. I was just going to suggest that the Chamber might want to take that report into consideration when evaluating all of the press stuff that's in this case, the radio stuff, the newspaper stuff. I have been harping from the beginning that it's not reliable, and now Ms. Korner has proven it to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ackerman. So, let's bring Mr. Radic. Shall we make a humungous effort and try to finish with it today.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I simply cannot can't. Just before he comes in, usher. Your Honour, it's quite clear that -- and I hope it's clear to Your Honours as well that this is perhaps from any point of view one of the most important witnesses Your Honours have heard from. I really have been through the matters to try and prune them down, but there are really a number of important matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So I will be definitely going into tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. And tomorrow I tried my best to shift the sitting to the morning, but I'm afraid I cannot. So we'll sit in the afternoon, and hopefully we'll finish early. Ms. Korner is sceptical.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So good afternoon to you, Mr. Radic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I take it that you have your spectacles with you today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I have them with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So let's proceed. You're testifying on the basis of your solemn declaration? Yes, you want to tell me something?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether it is customary for me to inform you of a change to part of my testimony yesterday -- mistake -- and enter the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You want to modify a part of your testimony, in other words?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's just one sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yesterday when I was asked about documents from Mr. Brdjanin, a document that had been signed in the capacity of coordinator, I said that the SDS, the municipal board of the SDS, had done that. The Prosecutor said you were also a member of the municipal board of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that very clearly. And you agreed to that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I automatically agreed to that since it was quite late already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I remember that very clearly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now I'm stating that I was never a member of the municipal board of the SDS. I checked that, and I was told -- I received this information from Banja Luka. I was told I was never a member of that board.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Yes, Ms. Korner. And may I remind you, you are still testifying under oath, under the solemn declaration that you entered the first day of your testimony. And if there is or are any questions that in your opinion would tend to incriminate you, you can address me straight away and bring that out and ask me for -- to be exempted from answering that question. And then, as I explained, we will take a decision whether that is the case or whether to apply a rule that we have to ask you to answer the question, just the same, with the caveats that our rules provide for. Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Arising out of what you just said, Mr. Radic, who did you talk to in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With my secretary. I asked him to check this, to check whether at any time I was a member of the SDS municipal board in Banja Luka. And later on, he told me that I had never been a member.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Are you saying that you're unable to recall yourself whether you were a member of the municipal board of the SDS in Banja Luka, together with Dr. Vukic?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In response to your question, when I was asked about the establishment of the crisis staff, I said that this was done by the SDS. And you told me that I was also a member of the SDS municipal board. I automatically replied that I had been a member. But later on, I remembered that in fact I was never a member of the SDS municipal board. So the error was mine.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you discuss any other aspects of your evidence?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I just wanted to check that because later on I remembered that I had really never been a member of the municipal board.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Because the reason I ask whether you discussed any other aspects of your evidence is I think you were told by His Honour at the end of the first day that you shouldn't talk about your evidence with anybody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You know that. You're aware of that obligation, no, of that duty, that you shouldn't talk to anybody about your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I said, it was my mistake when I gave this false testimony, when I gave the wrong testimony, and now I understand that I can't even do this. I can't even check this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. We may come back to that, Mr. Radic, but I want to move on, please, and deal with the Assembly of the Autonomous Region of Krajina. Could you have a look, please, at Document P23. These are the minutes or an extract from the minutes of the 9th session held on the 6th of November 1991. And there was a discussion -- or the agenda was the implementation of the conclusions adopted at the session held on the 26th of November 1991. That was -- we already dealt with yesterday, the day of the demonstration, and the day that there was apparently a meeting of the presidents of the municipality. And on the 6th of November under item 1, it was established that the presidents of the municipalities had failed fully to carry out the conclusions we adopted together at the last session. Those were the conclusions apparently contained in the telex. It was noted that in some municipalities, Sanski Most, Kotor Varos, Prijedor, Bosanska Krupa, and Bihac, it was impossible to implement these conclusions at all because they can only be carried out within the party. Now, you were at this session, Mr. Radic, because you spoke. If you look under item 2, you can see your speech. Is this the situation, that those instructions contained in that telex couldn't be carried out in those municipalities because there was no overall Serb majority in them?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just have a look to see which municipalities are concerned.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Directly under item 1, second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that that's the case. It says "Sanski Most, Kotor Varos, Prijedor, Krupa, Bihac." I assume that it wasn't possible to implement what had been requested; namely, the mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Based on the above, if you go down to the end of item 1, it was decided that the vice-president of the assembly of the autonomous region, Mr. Brdjanin, should inform the president of the Bosnia-Herzegovina SDS, Radovan Karadzic, as to the implementation. Now, was that because Mr. Brdjanin had more contact with Mr. Karadzic because he was a deputy?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably because the deputies had been elected, and it was their responsibility to communicate with the president and with the key figures in Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And the situation is, isn't it, Mr. Radic, that there was a lot of communication at this stage between the assembly of the autonomous region and the leadership of the SDS in Pale?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's difficult for me to confirm whether it was extensive or not. The president of the ARK could confirm that. The president of the autonomous region could confirm that and those who were given the task to communicate with the leaders in the Republika Srpska. Naturally, they had to communicate with the president and the leaders in Republika Srpska. That is quite natural.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, can you move, please, next -- I'm sorry, you can give that back to the usher. And could you look, please, now at Exhibit P31. This is the meeting that was held on the 8th of January. And there are two points that I want to raise. It was the meeting where Mr. Grahovac was dismissed. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember that really.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well, because a commission -- if you look, please -- I'm not sure where it appears. It's the last bit before the third effective item on the agenda. "A commission was formed to propose the president of the executive council of the autonomous region," and you were one of the members of the commission. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It says that Mr. Kupresanin, Predrag Radic, Predrag Lazarevic, Dusan Jaksic, and Radosav Vukic were there. At the session it was decided that they should speak to Slobodan Milosevic about the position of the Serbian people outside of Serbia. Yes, that's what it was about.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You, in fact, Mr. Radic, were quite an important member of this assembly, weren't you perhaps because of your position as president of the municipal assembly?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As president of the municipal assembly of the biggest town in Republika Srpska, and in that region, yes, I was. There were also two members of the club of intellectuals. That's Mr. Lazarevic, Dr. Jaksic, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I ask, what were you going to speak to Milosevic about, the position of the Serbian people outside Serbia. What was that about?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know, at the time it was already quite clear it was the 8th of January 1992. It was already quite clear that Bosnia and Herzegovina would secede from Yugoslavia. And we were interested, just as the Croats in Bosnia were interested, and they consulted their mother country, we wanted to see in our mother country, Serbia, what the position of Serbs in Krajina could be given that we were at a distance from the border with Serbia. So we wanted to see what their opinion of that subject was and whether it would be possible to find a satisfactory solution for those Serbs who were really threatened. They were very far away. They were to the west of the border, and we wanted to see what their fate would be. He must have had more information than we did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were you also interested to see whether Milosevic was prepared to lend support, financial and military, if necessary, to the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we did not discuss the military or financial support at the time. We discussed the general support to the Serbian People, which was separated from the rest. It was not our task to discuss military aid. It was our task to see what the -- our destiny might be and inform the Autonomous Region of Krajina, that is, the Assembly of the Autonomous Region of Krajina, about that. We did not discuss either military or financial decisions in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well, I want to show you now, please, a report in Sloboda Bosna. It's a disclosure, 2.468. So it's a new document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, if you haven't got it, perhaps you'd let us know. And that will be Exhibit 2700. What has Mr. Radic been given, the English or the B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just have a quick read through it. And then I just want to ask you a couple of questions.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just give me a moment, please. My name is mentioned in only one place here. I can't see anywhere that I said something or that I was on the team with these people.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Wait, Mr. Radic. It says that -- under the headline or the subheadline: "Helicopter raid on Belgrade." Do you see your name as part of the six-member delegation that went to see Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've said that I was on that team.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. But then the article goes on to describe the divergence of opinion within the Bosnian Krajina as to what course to take. And if you find that part in the article where it says: "Maybe the closest to the present view of Belgrade is the third or middle way, whose concept of regionalisation was rejected at the Sarajevo Assembly. The promoter of this option is Predrag Radic, with his collaborators, Professor Lazarevic and Dr. Jaksic, some of whom will very probably take up better, higher positions in the hierarchy of the Bosnian Krajina SDS or autonomous region." Do you see that part?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am looking at it, and it says here: "The first and the most radical one." Here I can't see anything. And I'm looking, and I'm looking to see where it says the relationship between Banja Luka and Sarajevo. Milosevic, Karadzic. I'm still looking for the place where it says that Brdjanin, Grahovac -- where is it? Where did you find that?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If you look, please, further on from what you're just reading, "the first and most radical," and then the second, and then the third. Your name appears as the promoter of the third option.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The third Yugoslavia, the second...

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness is reading aloud.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, please, you don't need to read it aloud. It's not very difficult. Just look down the article until you see your name.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see the second line where it says Vukic, Kupresanin, Brdjanin. Maybe I'm missing part of the article. I'm missing that third option that you have just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just continue reading where you said you were reading. And you will come across it. Just go on. But read to yourself without letting us hear your voice.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Radic, we're wasting time now. Have you found the passage or not?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't. I found the first one, the second one. And there is no third one. Maybe I am simply missing that part. You have said that it was a third mention, and that my name was mentioned next to it, but I can't see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Radic. We'll check and we'll get another copy if it has been cut off, but I want to move on because we're spending too much time on this. Do you agree with this, with what the article said, that there was a divergence of opinion as to how the Krajinas should -- how the Bosnian Krajina should exist within a Serbian State? First one that was being pushed by Dr. Babic; the second, Dr. Vukic, Mr. Kupresanin, and Brdjanin; and a third line, yours.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My approach was always very clear, and that was that joining the two Krajinas together would be very dangerous because Croatia was internationally recognised. And if that part was taken away from it and joined with this second part, then that would be like an annexation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Let's move on. Thank you. And we'll check to see whether that article is, in fact, complete. Now, I'd like you to look, please --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If you'd like, I can assist, Ms. Korner. It's directly under the photograph, the right-hand column directly under the photograph about a third of the way down.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Mr. Ackerman, but I want to move on. I think we've spent enough time on this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You can give that back, thank you, to the usher and I want you to now look at the very next meeting. No, there's one in between. The meeting on the 29th -- sorry, 24th of February, which is P32. This was the meeting, and I have no doubt you must -- well, I have no doubt. You recall, do you not, Mr. Radic, this meeting because this was the meeting where the proposal was made that there should be a Krajina republic?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was one of the options.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you yourself spoke, if you look, please, under item 1 and said words to the effect that it shouldn't be insinuated that anyone had anything against Karadzic, but the provisions of the draft constitution of the Serbian Republic were ridiculous. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't see it. Are we on page 4 or which page are we on here? When you say, item 1, I'm looking at it, but I don't see.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If you go down through the list of speakers, Brdjanin said quite a lot. Then a man called Vojo Bukalo, Gvero, Kupresanin, and then yourself.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Predrag Radic said that one shouldn't insinuate that somebody had anything against Karadzic, but that the solutions from the constitution of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina are ridiculous, and he advocated that some life should be added to this constitution so it should become binding on all the cantons in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That is exactly what I read to you a moment ago. It is not necessary for you to reread things. It's just taking up time. At the end of this meeting, a conclusion was adopted. If you look, please, under conclusion number 3, that's before the word "conclusion," that "various municipalities," and we see them listed, Banja Luka, Dubica, Gradiska, so on and so forth, "and parts of Krupa and Bihac should be proclaimed a sovereign republic which will establish relations directly with other parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina." Now, was that a solution with which you agreed?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say whether I agreed or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You mean you can't remember?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And the last -- there was another conclusion which concerned you; namely, that you, Kupresanin, and Erceg should go back to -- or hold discussions with the representatives of the government of the Republic of Serbia about delivery of oil derivatives and foodstuffs to the autonomous region. Item number 3, the newly constituted Serbian Municipalities joining the autonomous region. And then finally, at the very end, decision, please, can you look at that. "To send a memorandum about the genocide committed against the Serbian People to the Assembly of the Serbian People of Bosnia-Herzegovina was adopted unanimously." Can we take it from that that you voted for it if it was unanimous?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Usher, we don't have the relevant part of the text on the monitor.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's over the page, yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, this was to be sent to the United Nations, the memorandum about the genocide committed against the Serbian People, and this was adopted unanimously, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what was the purpose, as you say, of sending this to the United Nations about the genocide of the Serbian People?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To inform the United Nations about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what genocide were you talking about? In World War II?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Amongst other things, yes, because at that time there was -- the war had not started yet. Yes, to inform the United Nations about that particular genocide, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I see. All right. And finally -- not quite finally, but -- before we move to the next assembly meeting, could you have a look, now, please at Exhibit P34. Those -- this is a transcript of a meeting of the club of deputies on the 28th of February 1992. I know you were not a deputy, Mr. Radic, but did you attend any of the meetings of the club of deputies?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I can see that the -- this took place in Holiday Inn, and I wasn't there. Actually, I was there for a very, very brief time, and then I left because I was not given the floor and that's when I decided to walk away. It was almost midnight. I believe this was one of the last meetings that was held in the Sarajevo territory in February. Yes, now I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. So you were there for part of the time, but they wouldn't let you speak, so you left. That's what you're saying, is it?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's exactly what I said.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And the whole discussion was about, wasn't it, what you in the assembly in the Krajina had decided about this republic of the Krajina, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to refresh my memory, but I believe that this was the preparation for the walking out of the Serbian deputies from the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, they had already left, but never mind that. I want to ask you, please, because it's a long document --

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I want to ask you about some of the things that were said and see whether you heard them. Could you find the speech, please, of Mr. Kelecevic. In the English, it's at page 18.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which page?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In English, page 18. I can't help you, I'm afraid, in the Serbian document. I think it might be better if you give it to me and I'll find it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Witness is reading out names.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: He's found it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's the speech after -- there's Kasagic, after Kupresanin, and then Mr. Kelecevic. Do you see that? Did you know Mr. Kelecevic?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I knew him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you hear him say this: "My demand to my colleagues, the deputies, is that we distance ourselves from the statements of Mr. Radoslav Brdjanin. "Mr. Radoslav Brdjanin is causing a lot of damage to the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. deputies. He stated that we act in bad taste, that we do not act as befits deputies. Yesterday in Oslobodenje, he called for a vote of no confidence for the deputies from Krajina. Has he been manipulated and who has manipulated him, I don't know." And then he talks about Brdjanin managing to push the deputies at the assembly session to vote on what we voted on. Now, that was a reference back, wasn't it, to declare the republic of the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must say that I can't remember, and I couldn't remember before I read everything that Mr. Kelecevic said about Mr. Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Could you give me the document because I want to ask you about one other speech that was made and I'll find it for you. Here. Would you look, please, at Mr. Kontic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is page 28 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you know Mr. Marinko Kontic?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that this gentleman was from Kljuc, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know him that well. But I believe that he comes from Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well, one of the things he said in his speech was this: "The main problem in Banja Luka, and I will tell you who the people who need to be marked are, the president of the municipality, Radic, and Mr. Brdjanin, whom I have feared from day one." Do you have any idea what would have made Mr. Kontic say that?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I please read it? Does it say that anywhere here? Will you please tell me --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's the sixth --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sixth paragraph. I was going to tell him that. Is Marinko Kontic a witness for the Defence, Mr. Ackerman? Is he one of your witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I don't think so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Banja Luka, those who are not in our party are giving us problems. Is that that?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. You don't have to read it out. I just want to ask you if you have any reason to know why Mr. Kontic should have said that you and Mr. Brdjanin were the main problem in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I can't see my name here. Where is my name mentioned as being one of the main problems?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you have an extra copy of the B/C/S version, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could I have it back and I'll mark it. I can't mark the original. I'll point it out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I have the English one as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I want the bit that -- I don't think this is it. I want the bit that he's looking at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We're never going to finish like this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour is right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't have a copy of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you just... Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We've just marked it for you, your name and Mr. Brdjanin, Mr. Radic. Are you telling us you still can't see it?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Yes, I can. I can see it. But it says here the main problem is me. Why me? Probably I did not agree with him on something. And later on, it says that Mr. Brdjanin is also one of the problems. I have feared him from day one. And he doesn't say why he feared Mr. Brdjanin. But he does say that he had a few clashes with him. What clashes, I don't know. I must say that I did not have any clashes with this guy Kontic. Why does he consider me to be the main problem in Banja Luka? I really would be curious to have that clarified by him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So you're saying you can think of no reason why Mr. Kontic should have said that about you. That's your answer, is it?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know why I am his main problem. I'm sorry that I left the assembly. If I had heard him say that, I'm sure that I would have replied to him. Probably I did not allow him to do something in Banja Luka that he expected would be allowed. He was a deputy, and I suppose he expected that he could do in Banja Luka what he could do in Kljuc or I don't know where that was. But that's another story.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. You can give that document back to the usher now. And finally on the topic of the assemblies, and then we can move on to something else, could you have P35. Now, that's the extract of the meeting that followed the deputies' club meeting on the 28th. The deputies' club meeting on the 28th. On the 29th, Mr. Karadzic, Mr. Krajisnik, Mr. Koljevic, and Mr. Ostojic came to the assembly meeting. And do you recall this particular meeting, Mr. Radic, where effectively the assembly knuckled under and dispensed with the idea of a Krajina republic?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are assemblymen. And this is the minutes of the Assembly of the Autonomous Region of Krajina which was held on the 29th February in the great hall of the Banja Luka cultural centre, beginning at 1100 hours, and so on and so forth. I remember that they knuckled under, and that this subject, and particularly the constitution that I had the opportunity to see here, was no longer on the agenda. In simple terms, this was disallowed. The establishment was disallowed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Absolutely. So you clearly remember this. Now, I want to ask you about the conclusions. The first conclusion, if you can find that, please, was to this effect: "The deputies accepted the constitution of the Republic of the Serbian People in full." Then the status of the Autonomous Region of Krajina will be incorporated in the constitution of the republic. And then this, I want to ask you about this one: "Establish immediately strict control of the territory of the Autonomous Region of Krajina." What does that refer to?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What does control refer to? If something is part of Krajina, then it is obvious that there must be some sort of control. Everything that is to be discussed at the Assembly of AR Krajina, this should be the subject of control. I can't tell you exactly what had to be controlled, but they probably thought it was necessary to introduce some form of control in the ARK. I can't tell you what it concerns exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to say that here they adopted a constitution which was in accordance with the constitution of Republika Srpska, the constitution of the Serbian People. That's what it says in the first conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm not asking about that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about the first. It's the third one. What does it mean: "Establish immediately strict control of the territory"?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know. "Strict control," controlling the functioning, because it's obvious that up until then there was no control of the functioning of the municipalities in the ARK. That's perhaps what it concerns. But I really don't know what the subject of control was.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Wasn't it this: Let's look at the obvious, logical thing. That it was to take control of territories which had large populations of non-Serb, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where does it say so? Does it say that only non-Serbs had to be controlled? I can't see that here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. No, it doesn't say that, Mr. Radic. But that's what it meant, didn't it? That's what I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're making assumptions, and I can't confirm such assumptions on this basis.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I am making assumption which I am asking you as a person present at this meeting, whether that assumption is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, he's answered that twice now, I think. He said he's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think he's avoiding to answer. Let him answer. Because I am pretty sure that the witness knows that this third decision, or second or third, is the one out of three that were taken on that day, and they are all inter-related, so one follows the other, and this happens to be the last one. So given the first -- the previous decisions -- yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But he's already answered, Your Honour. "You're making assumptions and I can't confirm such assumptions on this basis." I guess he can say that again.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm asking -- leave aside the word "assumption." I am asking you, Mr. Radic, as a person who was present whether, in fact, this did not relate to seizing control of territories within the Krajina that had large populations of non-Serbs? Yes or no or I can't remember?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. But I would say that controlling the political and security situation in the ARK, which is the first item on the agenda, I think that this would have been a subject of incessant control. And we're still talking about the period prior to the war itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Radic. Let me ask you a very simple question: Does decision number 3 say "establish immediately strict control on the territory of the Autonomous Region of Krajina" or "of the territory of the Autonomous Region of Krajina"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Of the territory of the autonomous region" that's what it says, in order to see what is happening in that territory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: "Strict control of the territory"? It doesn't say "strict control of the organs of government or of institutions, or whatever, in the territory of the Autonomous Region of Krajina." It says "strict control of the territory" and I don't think that should confuse you much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says: "Establish strict control of the territory of the autonomous region immediately" because beyond the Sava, the Una, et cetera, fire had been opened -- fire had been directed at the territory of the region. So crossings of the Una and the Sava, that was the border between Croatia and ourselves, et cetera, so there had to be control. That is the control of territory that is being referred to, not people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Does it actually mean take control of the territory? Take control of the territory? Does it say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Establish control, not take control. Take it from whom?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you establish, you are going to establish control of a territory, still the same question arises. Look at those three decisions again, the first one, the second one, and the third one, because one follows the other. And tell me whether what was suggested to you by Ms. Korner in the beginning is actually what the only interpretation, only meaning that you could give to that third paragraph, that third decision.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't interpret it in the sense that people are to be controlled. The territory is to be controlled to prevent incursions into that territory. I can't accept the idea that people are to be controlled. And this can't be taken out of the context, inferred from the context. The deputies of the assembly accepted their constitution. It's not possible to take this out of context and say that control is to be established over people. And I want to stress yet again that at the time the war had not yet started.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. The war hadn't started, Mr. Radic, I agree with you. But what I'm suggesting is this: What was going on already was planning for the forceful takeover of municipalities. Now, is that right or is it not right?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't necessary to do that in Banja Luka. Let me tell you so immediately. As to what they were planning in other municipalities, don't ask me about that because that wasn't within my competence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But the whole idea of the assembly of the autonomous region and later the crisis staff, or one of the idea, was coordination between what was to happen in municipalities. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd like to see the conclusions from which such assumptions have been made.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm going to leave that subject, or just with one quick further document. Can you look, please, now at P119, two documents, in fact. It's a report in Glas about a press conference held after this assembly on the 29th of February. And could you find the part under "the end of dreams to become a ban" where you apparently said that the deputies "spat on Banja Luka." And then, please, read to yourself under the subheadline: "The SDS is playing with black pieces," everything you are alleged to have said, which is on page 2 of the English.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was after a session of the assembly which had been disrupted, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I just have one simple question. Did you say those things that you are reported as saying in the Glas newspaper?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm trying to find what I said here, yes. INTERPRETER: The witness is reading to himself again.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, don't read it aloud. Just read it yourself. And tell me when you've read it.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was a clash here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, simple question. Did you say the things that Glas reported you as saying? That's all I want you to say.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said several things here, not just one thing. Could you tell me what you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Is there anything there --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is there anything there --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- That you didn't say?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know, it's difficult for me to tell you. What I said has probably been recorded.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. It's right, isn't it, that by and large Glas accurately recorded what was said at press conferences and in the assembly?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By and large, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Right. That's all I want to ask you about those assembly meetings. But I want to ask one final question: Why did you tell us in interview in Banja Luka that you were not a member of the Autonomous Region of Krajina Assembly?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is this the document you're referring to, the one you've shown me?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Usher, can you take the document away.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I want you to look, because otherwise you'll ask me to show it to you, you'll see it on the screen, but we can give you the B/C/S version as well, at page 21 of the B/C/S version of your first interview.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think it's on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, it is, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You were asked this: "I want to know - and this is in the English at line 13 and in the B/C/S at line 16 - I want to know if you are telling us that at the same time as the crisis staff was in existence, so was the regional assembly." "I couldn't tell you that for sure," was your reply. "You'll need to find that in the documents." "Mr. Radic, you at the time were in Banja Luka. You were a member of the crisis staff, you were also a member of the assembly, were you not?" "I was not a member of the assembly." And I'm going to ask now that you look, please, at the next page, page 21, which is page 22 in the Serbian version, where the part that's in the crisis staff gazettes about the work of the autonomous region has the absolute support, at line 20, was put to you. And the question was: "Mr. Radic, do you agree on the 26th of May the assembly was not functioning?" "When was this done," you asked. Question: "On the 26th of May when this was issued, the assembly was not functioning." Again, you said, "I'd like to see the chronology of how the assembly was closed and how this was established because I was not in the assembly. I was not in the government, so I couldn't tell you." And on one last occasion, page 49 of the interview in English, and it's page 51 in B/C/S, if we can put those up, the question at line 19 in the English of page 49: "The regional assembly did not meet after April of 1992, did it?" And you said: "That would be very difficult for me to confirm, but it's very strange that the executive body would be meeting. I mean, who did they answer to seeing that it's the executive body of the assembly." Question: "I'm asking you if you were aware that they did not meet." Your answer: "No I was not a member of the assembly. I was not a member of the executive committee or whatever you want to call it because simply I was not elected into it." Now, on no less than three occasions during your interview in Banja Luka, you told us you were not a member of the regional assembly. Why did you do that? Apparently there was a fourth, but never mind. Why did you tell us in Banja Luka in 2001 that you were not a member of the regional assembly, but in actual fact as we've just seen you played a major part in the proceedings?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll repeat this, what we read in the newspaper a minute ago. That's what we wanted to do. But if you're asking me about the assembly that was established and the executive committee which was also elected, I wasn't a member of the executive committee of the assembly of ARK. I didn't attend those sessions, and I wasn't elected. And they didn't elect me, although I had been proposed as a minister for agriculture.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Are you telling us that your saying you were not a member of the assembly on three or four occasions was simply meant to indicate that you were not a member of the executive council or the government?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't a member of the government.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'll try one more time. Why did you tell us - nothing to do with the government - that you were not a member of the assembly itself?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By virtue of my position, I had been proposed as a member of the assembly, as the president of the municipal assembly. But I didn't attend those assembly sessions. I didn't even come when I was supposed to be elected as the minister of agriculture for the ARK. That's a fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I suggest to you, Mr. Radic, you denied that you were a member of the assembly to us in Banja Luka because you knew that that assembly was planning the beginnings of the takeovers, the crimes, in the Autonomous Region of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd like to see where I said that I recognised that it would be an organ that would prepare to commit crimes. I'd like to see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm not going to pursue this point any longer.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I want to move, Your Honour, to a different topic. I know, perhaps, it's a little early, but if we could take the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, we'll have a 20-minute break starting from now. We'll resume at 5 to 4.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Radic, I think I need to make it clear to you that if we continue proceeding at this slow pace, you'll probably still be here Wednesday of next week. So I suggest you take the advice I gave you on the first day, don't go around in circles. Just answer the questions that are put to you. Most of them have been questions that only required a yes or no answer. Because otherwise, I mean, we will be here. It's only two other witnesses that have scheduled for next week will probably stay waiting. But I'm not going to stop Ms. Korner. So I suggest that you take my advice, and you be concise and precise in your answers so that we can send you home end of this week. Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could you shown, please, Exhibit -- I'm sorry, it's a new disclosure. 2.583.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, this is a document signed by Mr. Blagojevic with the stamp of the assembly of the autonomous region. It's dated 21st of March. It's addressed to -- the translation says the chairman, but I imagine it's the president of the Serbian Democratic Party, president of the executive council of the municipal assembly, president of the municipal assembly, and members of the main board of Bosnia-Herzegovina SDS. So you qualified under two heads, as president of the municipal assembly and a member of the main board. "Please note that your presence is obligatory at the session of the main board of the BH Serbian Democratic Party. The session will be held at 1700 hours on the 23rd of March 1992 in Sarajevo. You must bring along a geographical map of your municipality with the national boundaries and the decision on accession into the Autonomous Region of Krajina." First, do you remember getting this document?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Which, Your Honour, I think will be P2701.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is it 270 -- yeah, okay. Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to you inquire how long the OTP has had this document, why it was not disclosed in disclosure under Rule 66. And if there's not a good explanation, then I object to its being used at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I can't possibly give an explanation, Your Honour. I don't know how -- where this document comes from at the moment or how we got it. I think the answer is under what head should it have been disclosed. We weren't going to use it before, and I don't think we were. We didn't have to disclose it. So I mean -- sorry, Mr. Ackerman. I'm slightly taken aback by the objection. But we did not intend to use this document at the stage during the Prosecution case. Therefore, I assume it wasn't disclosed. But as to how long we've had, or where it comes from, at the moment I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The disclosure requirements of the Prosecutor have nothing to do with whether they intend to use a document or not, Your Honour. That's only the Defence requirements. It's clearly helpful to the presentation of the Defence. Falls clearly within Rule 66, and it should have been turned over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Under which part of the 66, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Judge, I don't have the rule in front of me. It might be 66(C).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 66(C) is when the Prosecution can ask the Trial Chamber for exemption.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'd have to look at the rules. I don't know the rules off the top of my head.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Registrar or usher, you can give the rules to Mr. Ackerman. I think Ms. Korner is right, if it's not a document. Anyway, have a look at 66. And in the meantime, Ms. Korner can find out when -- what's the origin of -- wasn't even used in the --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: 66(B), Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: "The Prosecution shall on request permit the Defence to inspect any books, documents, photographs, and tangible objects in the Prosecutor's custody and control which are material to the preparation of the Defence."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you make a request for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I did. I made a request under Rule 66(B) for disclosure, and it triggered reciprocal. So she had to turn all this over. And they did, they gave us thousands and thousands and thousands of pages of documents that they never intended to use, but they were in the Prosecutor's view helpful to the presentation of the Defence. And I can show you, I must have 40.000 pages of material that they have not ever used and never will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you exclude that you have this as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yeah, I know I don't have this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I say that the request was specific, as it had to be. We were asked to provide, and did, the documents seized from the Banja Luka buildings; namely, the municipal CSB 1st Krajina Corps. That was a specific request. I mean, clearly, 66(B) doesn't entitle you to say "everything that you've got." You have to be specific. And those were the requests made. I think -- I'm rather thinking this comes from one of the collections. But Your Honour, I don't know. We could spend a lot of time on this. I don't mind, because it's a lead-in to another document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the moment, I think we ought to go ahead. I don't agree with you, Mr. Ackerman, or at least with the interpretation you have given to 66(B) even if you made a request.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Unless you were given the opportunity to inspect, and I underline the word "inspect" and this was hidden from you. If that is the case, yes, we have something to discuss. But if it's not the case, I think we ought not to lose time on it now, and I reserve your position until later.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Radic, after that interruption, did you get this letter?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have never taken any maps to any meetings at this place referred to in here, which means that either I did not receive this letter or -- in any case, I didn't take a map with me. It is possible that the president of the municipal board had one on him, but I didn't have a map on me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Radic. Are you saying that you in Banja Luka didn't receive a copy of this letter, though you qualified under two heads?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't get it, otherwise I would have had to bring a map. And if I'd done that, I would have remembered it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have remembered taking a map to a meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. But attend a meeting, then, on the 23rd of March, whether you took a map or not, in Sarajevo at the SDS club?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only once was I there, during the elections. When that was, I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well, I'd like you to have a look, please, at a document, P26.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I take it that document is temporarily exhibited until such time as Mr. Ackerman has decided what he wants to do?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I've made my objection. I don't think I need to go beyond it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: These are the minutes of the 12th session of the Assembly of the Serbian People held in Pale on the 24th of March.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In English.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, you should have them in the Serbian language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Turn the page just in case it's on the back.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. First question is, did you go?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Allow me to just briefly look at this document to --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- Refresh my memory.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, while the witness is doing that, we've done a check. We acquired the document in Bihac on the 8th of October 1995. So it wouldn't have been included, Your Honour, I make that absolutely clear, in the documents that Mr. Ackerman made an application for under 66(B). As to why we haven't disclosed it before or used it, I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just want to make sure --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is not the only one.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I made a special application because of the seizures that they did, to have those materials, even though they probably didn't fall under 66(B). The basis of that request was that since they had removed all the documents that I would have in the course of my investigation tried to find myself, that they became the repository of those documents, and therefore they were the only source for me to look at that material. That's a totally different thing from a Rule 66 request for materials in the possession of the Prosecutor helpful to the preparation of the Defence. And that was clearly -- that was made very clear at the time, and huge, huge, disclosure, as you know, because I would show you piles, was made under Rule 66(B) to me because of that request. And this should have been part of it. They've had it since 1995, and it clearly is relevant to this case.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't think I can say anything further myself, Your Honour. I don't agree with Mr. Ackerman's interpretation, but I don't think it's -- of what he asked for, but I don't think it's helpful to rehash all the old history. That's the situation. It wasn't apparently disclosed, and we've now got it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But this is on the face of it a document which isn't going to change much. But I don't want to come across a document later on which can be fundamentally important and which was similarly not disclosed. So --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'd love to be able to say, Your Honour, it won't happen, but I really -- I can't. But we did -- all I can say, is we have done our level best to comply with all our disclosure obligations. But obviously this document or the reason for it wasn't appreciated at the time. It doesn't directly relate to Mr. Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, it doesn't. And that's until the rule that Mr. Ackerman is basing himself upon remains as it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, as I say, I don't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. As I say, I think I've said all I can say on it, and if I can perhaps leave it to Your Honours and Mr. Ackerman if you wish to take the matter further.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, you've obviously been given an opportunity to look through it. Did you attend this session?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was never invited to the sessions of the People's Assembly of Republika Srpska. It would be deputies who would go there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Because you see, one of the things that was said, again, the verification of the -- well, there were two things. It's pages 22 and 23 of the English. If you give me, please, the Serbian version, usher, otherwise we're going to be here for a long time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would just like to make the observation that the tenor of events in this courtroom today has been that these problems are all Mr. Radic's fault. And if the Prosecution had taken these B/C/S documents and marked the place they want Mr. Radic to look at, we would have moved much faster. This process of having to spend five or six or eight minutes while they try to find the part in the B/C/S they want him to look at is what's taking up an enormous amount of time here. And if we're here until Monday, that would just be outrageous, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, could you have a look, please, at this page of the document. It's the end of Dr. Karadzic's speech at this session where he was discussing the police force. And do you see the following words: "How to separate the police force, take the resources that belong to the Serbian people and take command. The police must be under the control of the civilian authority. It must obey it. There is no discussion about that. That's the way it must be." It's on page 22 of the English. Do you see those words?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. How to separate the police force.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: One of the things that was discussed, wasn't it, in the assembly of the autonomous region and in the assembly at the republic level was how there was to be a new Serbian MUP and how the municipalities, which were not Serb controlled, should control the police force? That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I read here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And that was clear, wasn't it? The police at all levels had to come under the control of the civilian authority?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the document doesn't say that at all. If Ms. Korner is referring to the document, it doesn't say that. The army and the police and everybody at the top had a civilian control. I mean, that's the way governments work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, you shouldn't have intervened.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I really do object to objections that give the witness the answer. The question I asked was a very clear one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please repeat it, Ms. Korner. And the witness needs to have a look again at those three, four lines and give us his answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, the question I'm asking you, Mr. Radic, is this: That at the top and at the SJB level, the police came under the control of the civilian authority. At the top, the republic controlling the MUP; at the bottom, the municipality assemblies controlling the police.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You don't agree with that. All right.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Radic, we can move on. And I now want to deal with the arrival of the SOS. You've already looked --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would just like to because of my objection, and I was a bit criticised for making it, I think it should be made clear to the Chamber that this same question was asked of Mr. Radic over and over during the Prosecutor's interview with him, and he repeatedly said the police were not under any civilian control.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to that comment as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, it's passed. The topic --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm going to be returning --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Ms. Korner had accused me of giving him the answer, but it was an answer that he had given many times before during his interview with the Prosecution. So I didn't give him the answer --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, what happened during the interview, I don't know because I wasn't there. It doesn't seem to me however that at that particular part the witness was faced or shown the document that he had in front of him, and he still has in front of him, and that certainly could have changed the situation completely.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour -- I don't think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's forget it for the time being and let's move ahead, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The document that you had, Mr. Radic, can go, and it has now gone. You've already looked with Mr. Ackerman at the demands that were made by this group called the SOS. Now, do you agree, Mr. Radic, that the SOS arrived in Banja Luka on the morning of the 3rd of April, surrounded the municipal building, and set up barricades in various parts of Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you agree that these men were armed?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you agree that they wore some kind of paramilitary military?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of them, yes. Some of them, no. Some wore uniforms; some didn't. Some even wore civilian hats on their heads.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you agree that these men were thugs?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, some of them were thugs, yes. There were thugs amongst them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: They were criminals? They included known criminals in their numbers?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't say -- I didn't say they were criminals. Their behaviour was dodgy and they were of a low morale. Whether they were criminals, I wouldn't dare say that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, you were asked about this in the interviews in Banja Luka, in both interviews. And if I can just find my note on that. Yes, on page 63 of the first interview, and it's page 64 in the B/C/S, and we'll put it up on the screen. Usher, can you give -- what have you put up there, the B/C/S version? Give it to the witness. All right. At line 25 of the English, page 63, same version of the same question: "They were armed and were paramilitaries. Is that correct?" "I cannot call them anything military because they were not military. They were just thugs."

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I used the word "aroba" [phoen] which would equal "thugs."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe robbers.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter apologises, does not understand word in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We may have a slight problem. But anyhow, thugs, robbers, whatever. And then they issued these demands, Mr. Radic?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Which, as we saw from the article in the newspaper, were accepted by you as the mayor of Banja Luka. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not all of them were accepted. Not all of them could be accepted. How could I accept to talk to the army, that is, to the main staff of the army of Yugoslavia and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm going to come on to each individual demand in a moment. You accepted those that you could accept. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to see all of the demands one by one, and then I would be able to tell you which demands I accepted, which I couldn't accept, because I can't remember all of the things that were demanded.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I tell you, I'm going to get back to it, but you actually went Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. through each and every demand with Mr. Ackerman during your evidence on, I believe, the -- yes, the first day -- it was virtually the first day you were asked by Mr. Ackerman. And from page 7 of the LiveNote, quite a long way through. So you did go through it, but I'm going to take you back. You did accept some of the demands. Can you take it from me that's what you told us?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What could be accepted, I accepted. We accepted that we would investigate whether there was any crime in the municipality, that I would go and talk to the main staff of the army of Yugoslavia, that I guaranteed that the law on this or that would be implemented. I can't remember all of the demands, but whatever was acceptable we accepted.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mr. Radic.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like you to remind me of those demands first.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I will. But I want you to answer one simple question first: Why did you accept any of the demands from this band of armed criminals?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, did I have any choice?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, why didn't you call in the army and the police?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that at the time, the army and the police, the army was regrouping for the corridor, and the police was aware of that. The police should have intervened. I can ask the police to do something, but I wasn't in a position to give them any orders.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But you didn't even ask the police to do anything, did you?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police was aware of what was happening in the town.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, answer the question I asked you, please. Did you ask the police to --

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. Perhaps I did ask them to come and intervene. But it's obvious that there was no intervention because they had blocked the radio station and all the institutions. They were blocked, crossroads, the roads, the checkpoints that had been set up, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm told that 43, line 12 where it says: "That I would go and talk to the main staff of the army of Yugoslavia" what he really said was: "How could I go and talk to the main staff of the army of Yugoslavia?" In other words, he saying he didn't do it I think because he didn't have the authority to do it. That's what I'm told he said.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm perfectly happy for Mr. Ackerman to correct something like this, but not to add on why he thinks he said it. Your Honour, I agree, but that could have been corrected when we get to the tape being checked because that's what we all heard him say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, you're both right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Radic, why didn't you go and say to Mr. Zupljanin or to Mr. Tutus "Why are you not doing something to clear these criminals"?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were informed of their presence. So I wasn't in a position to give the police any orders. They could have received an order according to the chain of command to deal with it. I couldn't give the orders. Municipal representatives didn't give the police orders, either before the war, during the war, or after the war. They were well aware of what was happening.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you keep on saying that, Mr. Radic. For the moment, let's take it as you say, that you couldn't give orders to the police. Are you telling us that you couldn't say to Mr. Zupljanin or any of the other people that I have named "Why are you not doing anything about these men? Contact your superiors in Pale"?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were informed. I informed them of what was happening. And as to what they would go on to do, I don't know about that. I don't know what they did afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Wasn't the truth that this was an SDS-planned incursion into Banja Luka? That's why nobody did anything about it.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I already said who -- I've already said on several occasions that I don't know who organised all of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. But it was absolutely clear, wasn't it, that this wasn't some, as it were, lawless band of men suddenly arriving; this was an orchestrated action?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
