utterances.text: They had someone's support, but I don't know whose because I don't know. But they must have had someone's support. As they blocked the municipal assembly, the radio, and everything else, given these blockades, they must have had someone's support.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And the army did nothing?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And the police did nothing?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that at a meeting when they were making their requests, I think there were police representatives there, and I think that there is a list of the persons who attended that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Why did you agree to go on to this crisis staff that was -- that they asked for?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The crisis staff was their main condition for entering the municipal assembly of Banja Luka and the Assembly of the ARK. That was their request. They had to have their representatives there. Why did I accept that? Well, that's one of the reasons. And why the assembly accepted that, that's something else.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, I want to know why you personally agreed to go on a crisis staff demanded by this band of thugs rather than refusing?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There weren't that many of them there. You can see that on the list. You can see how many of them were in that crisis staff. There were people who were reliable in that crisis staff, so to speak. If you have a look at the list, I can tell you who they were. There are one or two of these people.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The list that we've already been through included one of the top representatives of the army, Colonel, later General Kelecevic. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was also on the list of those who were requested to be in the crisis staff. There were some judges, and there were other prominent people from the town of Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Absolutely. And what I want to know from you, Mr. Radic, as a member of this crisis staff and as a person who was there, was why all these top-level people agreed to go on a crisis staff demanded by these thugs?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know, someone had to calm [Realtime transcript read in error "come down"] them down. It was better for such people to be there, rather than having people brought in from the street and taken to the crisis staff. Their action gradually diminished in strength. All their requests were quite simply not adopted.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well, I'm going to go through those requests now. Can you have, first of all, the list of requests which is Exhibit P134. That's already an exhibit. And then I'm going to ask you to have a look at another document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then, Your Honour, I'm going to, because this is the best --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: 47, line is it 14? 47, line 4. He said: "You know, someone had to calm them down," not "come down." I think that makes a difference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. Mr. Radic, have you heard Mr. Ackerman? Were you paying attention to what he was saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, someone had to calm them down, someone had to have the authority to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The transcript said that you had said something different. So yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm going to show you what you said. It's not in the newspaper, but it was taken down by -- on the radio.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is 2326. And I'll have it put out on the ELMO. It's part of Exhibit 2326, the diary dated the 3rd of April. Hang on a minute, please. And page 6 can go on to the ELMO in English, and I will find that in the B/C/S version, I hope. Yes, here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Radic --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, just to be consistent, I'll make the same objection I made yesterday, that she is using statements of witnesses which I was not permitted to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: She is not using a statement of witnesses. This is an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm using, because it's the best record we have, the document which is an exhibit in this case which will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stop, Ms. Korner. Please proceed. Your objection has been recorded, put on record. I don't agree with you. This is an exhibit that is being shown to the witness. It recounts on the face of it the events that took place on those days, and he is going to be asked a question. And you shouldn't even mention that this may have been used by a witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have to make a proper objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, it's -- you ought to be able to distinguish between a document which is an exhibit, piece of evidence already from the direct testimony of a witness, which cannot be put --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If I made a transcript an exhibit, then I could ask questions about what somebody said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, of course not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Because that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. This is not a transcript of evidence. This is documentation on which evidence was based.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: She is getting the same place through the back door that she can't get through the front door, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't agree with you, Mr. Ackerman. Anyway, your objection is put on record. Ms. Korner, I don't need any explanations from you. Please proceed with your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, did you go on to Banja Luka Radio to explain about the SOS? Are you listening, Mr. Radic?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. Please, refresh my memory. If it says so here, then I must have gone there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were blocking the radio. They wouldn't allow me to go.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. I'll show you -- Mr. Radic, we can spend a lot of time here, but will you take it from me, you did go on Banja Luka Radio, you were reported in the newspaper as saying so, and I'm saying this is a record of what you actually said. Are you prepared to accept that, or do you want to look at the newspaper?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, now I see that it says at about 5.00, Radio Banja Luka informed about the request of the SOS et cetera --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, please, again, answer yes or no. It's as simple as that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He doesn't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If I show you a newspaper report, will you accept it from me that you went on to Banja Luka Radio?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it says that I was present, in that case, you'll refresh my memory, and I can say yes. But I can't remember whether I went to the radio or when I was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well, I suggest you went on to the radio on the -- either the 3rd or the 4th. I think it's probably the 3rd. Now, you began what you had to say, Mr. Radic, according to this record of what you said, that "the SOS imposed a blockade and demanded that the Banja Luka Crisis Staff be set up where the frontline fighters could put forward their demands and of course the meeting of these demands could be negotiated." And then you explained that the primary motive was the letter that Mr. Doko had sent to the municipal assemblies. Do you remember saying something like that?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then you explained how you had formed the crisis staff, and then you gave all the names of those people on the crisis staff.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I just want to ask about one more name. Nenad Stevandic was there on behalf of the political structures. What political structures?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had asked that Vukic be there for the SDS, and Nenad Stevandic at the time must have been the president of the Serbian Sokol, or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. And then you went through each of the demands. Number 1, and you can confirm them against the list of the demands, was that the interior -- the law on interior affairs of the Serbian Republic be implemented as soon as possible. And then you said there was an amendment made on the territory of Banja Luka CSB, not only Banja Luka, but the entire CSB, that the insignia be changed and that staff loyal to the Serbian Republic of BH and Yugoslavia be appointed. And then you said: "As this was the first amendment, as it was initially requested, this be done on the territory of Bosanska Krajina since this was implemented on the territory of Banja Luka, we have no right to talk on behalf of Bosanska Krajina. This will probably be done by the AR Krajina organs." Do you agree that you said that?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were their requests. I've stated what their requests were, and that was -- that information was provided. It says that these were their requests in the newspapers. I only relayed their requests.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. But you were saying, this is the amendment we're making. It can only be done in Banja Luka by us. For the rest of the Krajina territory it will have to be done by the Krajina organs.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. Because there were representatives of the police who said that they would implement what it said, what was stated in the law. They had the law, and it was necessary to implement it. The SNF Krajina would decide on who would implement it in Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can we go on to demand number 2: "The supreme command and the presidency of Yugoslavia not break up the Banja Luka corps..." And so on and so forth. And what you said on radio, I suggest, was this, that -- and these were your words: "We warn of a large number of officers in the Banja Luka Corps" -- is that what they were saying? Sorry. No, that's what they were saying. You were reading out what they said. What you actually said was your conclusion: "The Presidency and General Staff will be informed about this conclusion as early as Monday through direct contact with the crisis staff representative, Nenad Stevandic, and the conclusion will be submitted in written form." Do you agree that's what was decided?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That it should be sent to the general Staff and the Presidency of Yugoslavia. Yes, that was concluded, and it must have been implemented, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Number 3, request the arrest of war profiteers, et cetera, and you say this demand was also adopted. Number 4, it's requested that the staff in Jugobanka, Banja Luka and Privredna Bank company, be dismissed in order for a monetary coup to be prevented. This inclusion is to be adopted by the 6th of April. All right? Item number 6: "Municipal organs be re-examined." You stated: "That the 6th conclusion" -- I'm sorry, yes. Sorry, the fifth. I'm sorry, it's my fault. The fifth conclusion: "We demand that staff be dismissed in the post where those who voted against Yugoslavia are employed as managers or operators or technical officers, and therefore cannot work for the Yugoslav PTT community." That conclusion -- and then the sixth was to request the work of the municipal organs be re-examined. That sixth conclusion which is to be implemented by Radoslav Brdjanin, Milinkovic and Mitrakovic goes as follows: "Dismissal of managers conducting anti-Serb policy is requested in all public companies. We call upon the workers to schedule staff meetings, shareholders, and implement those demands." And so on and so forth. Now, what I want to ask you about this, where in the demands that the SOS gave you did it say that all managers conducting anti-Serb policy is requested in all public companies? Because conclusion number 5 -- I'm sorry, request or whatever it was. Request number 5 says: "We request replacements in the post office and in the PTT." It's the same thing. Where is there a demand of a dismissal of managers conducting an anti-Serb policy in all public companies?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where does it say they will be dismissed in all public companies?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. You on radio said to the public in Banja Luka Radio -- in Banja Luka, sorry, that the sixth conclusion which was to be implemented by Mr. Brdjanin, Mr. Milinkovic, and Mr. Mitrakovic -- do you see that in the document? Not in the demands.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just want to object to the form of the question. Ms. Korner said "you said on radio," blah, blah, blah, blah. The proper question is someone who wrote this down claims that you said on the radio such and such, I think. I think that's a fairer question. And while I'm up, page 52, line 16, he didn't say that "it must have been implemented." He said "it probably had been implemented."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: He probably doesn't even know where we're talking about. It's back when we're talking about the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I take your word for it, Mr. Ackerman. Let's proceed. Let's move ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If we're going to have an argument about this, can you also have, please, P137.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: On the ELMO, please, page -- the fourth page of the English version. No, wrong page. Usher, if you -- can you just put my copy of the highlighted version on the ELMO, rather than going through this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. According to Glas, and that's just a summary of what we've just been dealing with, the crisis staff entrusted a working group consisting of Brdjanin, Mitrakovic, and Milinkovic to make arrangements by the 15th of April this year for initiating legal procedure for the dismissal of all key officials in Banja Luka enterprises who are pursuing an anti-Serbian policy. Now, where in the demands that were made by the SOS did they demand the dismissal of all anti-Serbian officials in Banja Luka enterprises? Take it from me, Mr. Radic, they didn't.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After item 5, because I have three documents here. One is the one I've got here. The second one is also in front of me, and the third one is the one I'm holding in my hands. I'd like to read something out here. Under 6: "They accepted item 6, although he was on Radio Banja Luka, he didn't read it out." This has to do with item 5. The deadline was the 10th of April. The PTT director was responsible for that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please slow down when reading. The interpreter cannot follow.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was not what was read out on the radio.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right, I'm going to ask you, Mr. Radic --

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that that had to be done.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry. You didn't say on radio, is that what you say, that --

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just a moment. -- that a commission -- that the decision to be implemented by Brdjanin, Milinkovic, and Mitrakovic, "the dismissal of all managers conducted by the anti-Serb policy is requested in all public companies." Are you saying that you never said that on radio?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It says here that that request of the SOS organisation was accepted. That's the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but it's being put to you, Mr. Radic, that SOS, the SOS, never made that request. The only request that there is in this context or in that context is number 5, relating to the PTT, the post, telephone, and telegraphy, and it had nothing to do with all public companies, and all those were not following the Serb course, or damaging it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The simple point is this, Mr. Radic, and it's taking a long time to get to it. Why did you go further, you and your cohorts, go further than the SOS had actually asked?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you sure that what you read in Glas is verbatim what -- or not verbatim what was demanded from the SOS?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, but I'm suggesting that what's contained in this document about your radio broadcast is verbatim, or more or less verbatim, and that you said on the radio that Mr. Brdjanin, Mr. Milinkovic, and Mr. Mitrakovic would adopt a conclusion that managers adopting an anti-Serb policy in all public companies would be dismissed.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that Radio Banja Luka was blocked. They received the demands that were supposed to be read out, and it says here, demand number 6 was adopted. And although it was on radio Banja Luka, it wasn't read out. We are talking about item 1 -- the conclusion number 6 was handed to them, but was never read out. So this is not my interpretation, but this is what the SOS had delivered to Banja Luka Radio when it blocked it, and this should also have been read out, but it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In all fairness, Ms. Korner, the paragraph from Glas, relative paragraph, actually starts with the words "during the negotiations, another resolution was reached." So it seems to me that what was in the -- that this was not amongst the original demands made by SOS, but was an addendum to which they arrived at following further negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'll ask the witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please go ahead. But that's how I understand it. That's how I read it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That could be anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But anyhow, is this right, Mr. Radic, that during the negotiations, as it was put, the SOS asked not just for the post office workers be dismissed but workers, anti-Serb, so-called anti-Serbian workers in all enterprises?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's why I said that not all of their demands are here in the newspaper, in Glas. There were other things that were said that were never supposed to be done, and those things were read out on the radio.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you explain to me why you agreed to even greater demands made by the SOS which were wholly and utterly illegal?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, it's up to you to decide whether or not they're illegal, not Ms. Korner's decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner is suggesting to him that they were illegal.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic said yesterday it was an illegal decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He has already stated that the decision to dismiss persons like what was his name, the director of Metal, I forgot his name.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Osmancevic, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Osmancevic was illegal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: My other objection is that that question has two questions in it. Why did you agree to greater demands, and were they illegal? If he says "yes," he's saying yes to both of those and he may not want to say yes to both of those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, that's true. Let's take them one by one. And the first one is, again, relative, Ms. Korner, because if the new demand was made during the negotiations, well, you put it at par, and it was accepted together with the rest.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think may be Your Honour is not following what I'm putting.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: These demands that are listed there do not contain that demand to sack all managers. Do you agree with that, Mr. Radic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have been here three times now. He said just a few moments ago that's why he was saying it's not on that list of demands. I think that's clearly established and we're now wasting time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's get this over and done with. The decision to sack all key officials in Banja Luka enterprises who were not pursuing -- or who were pursuing an anti-Serbian policy was not amongst the demands that were first put to you by the SOS. Is that correct, or not? That's a yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So next thing. So why did you accept it, or why did you take that decision? It is being put to you that you were not only prepared to take over, accept all the suggestions or all the demands of the SOS, but that you even went beyond.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't make any decisions. This was done under the pressure of that group which took the municipal building, the radio, and many other buildings in Banja Luka. What decisions could I have taken in that position? Everybody was clear that this was illegal. I told you already that those decisions or demands were never enforced or implemented.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner. He's opened another chapter again for you. He has just told you that those decisions were illegal and they were not implemented in any case.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: How can you even start to say that, Mr. Radic? That decision to sack all the managers -- the so-called anti-Serbian one, was the major one that was brought into effect, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you have any proof that all this was put into effect immediately after that?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You say "immediately." If you mean they were all sacked in one go, no, they weren't. But gradually, slowly but surely, starting in April, managers like Mr. Osmancevic were sacked. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Osmancevic was sacked and replaced by another man. Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, the point that has taken us so long to get here, Mr. Radic, is this, isn't it, the reason there was a further increase of these demands is because they were there to carry out the SDS policy, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether this was the SDS policy. But it was put in there that this is how things should be done. Whether this was an SDS policy, I wouldn't be able to tell you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And shortly after this, Mr. Brdjanin started to go into the media explaining that named people, including Mr. Osmancevic, including Colonel Hasotic from the army, including Colonel Kranjc, various other people, should be dismissed, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: When you were asked by Mr. Ackerman at page 27 of the LiveNote for the 3rd of November why you hadn't had the army and police arrest these men and throw them out of town, you gave a number of reasons. You said first if you look at the date when all of this was happening, you'll see this was happening when the army was withdrawing from Slavonia. And then you said this: "I would also like to remind you and I'm sure you'll find it in a document somewhere that at that time 12 babies died in a clinical hospital centre. They were prematurely born babies, and they died only because they couldn't get oxygen." Now, do you want to stick by that that answer, that at the time that the SOS came in on the 3rd of April, this is when the so-called Banja Luka babies -- well, not so-called. The Banja Luka babies apparently died?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, not all 12 of the babies died in one day because of the SOS. They died because the borders were closed and they could not receive the oxygen in the incubators where they were. Please do not try to say that I said that it all happened on one day. They died. You know what their names are. Their graves. And please, do not -- this really doesn't make any sense, and I didn't say that this happened because of the SOS came on that day, but because there was no oxygen and because we were blocked and we couldn't get oxygen at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, I read you back your exact words, and I now want to deal once and for all in this case, I hope, with the Banja Luka babies. I want you to look, first of all, at an edition of Glas.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wish we could deal once and for all with the issue of the Banja Luka babies because somebody would be held responsible for that case.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just want to enter an objection again about a document that wasn't previously turned over that clearly is relevant to this case. We have been talking about Banja Luka babies since probably about the first day of the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is a public document, an edition of Glas, and we offered Mr. Ackerman the facilities to go through all our editions of Glas --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: She is right. She is right. I withdraw the objection. She is absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, both of you. Ms. Korner, let's not make an issue out of it. Let's move ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I'll resist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I also notice the witness is getting tired.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: As I say, if Your Honour wants to adjourn --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no. I'll stop only if Mr. Radic says he wants to. But I can read the expression on his face that he is getting tired. And I think I have enough experience to know if a person is getting tired or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't want to take any unfair advantage of Mr. Radic. If he feels that he would prefer to adjourn, then I'll ask Your Honour to adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, are you feeling tired?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is disgusting to show a document like this. I am not tired. I am prepared to continue and explain why I mentioned the case of these babies in my testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's continue. The moment you feel tired and you need to stop, let me know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I want to deal just with this aspect of it. This is an article -- can I just see -- article dated the 4th of June where Glas is reporting that as of tomorrow the fate of seven babies in an incubator could be a terrible one and deals with the fact of the lack of oxygen. Do you agree that is the 4th of June, two months after the arrival of the SOS?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were blocked even at the time when the SOS came. I mentioned this just as an example of what was happening in this confined space which was referred to as Krajina. So this is just one example to illustrate what was going on. Obviously, there was a lack of medicines. There was a lack of food and all the other things, and then soldiers started withdrawing from the front lines --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, all that I'm asking you about is having seen this article, do you accept that the Banja Luka babies had nothing to do with the difficulties you had or you say you had in getting rid of the SOS?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, this indeed did not yet happen. But this just illustrates our situation, and all the things that were happening and that could happen in this enclosed space.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could that be made 2702, please, P2702. Could you look, please, at the next article dated the 8th of June from Glas.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Reporting that the oxygen has arrived from Belgrade to Banja Luka. Do you remember that, the flight from Belgrade to Banja Luka with the oxygen?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was such a small quantity that it was used within the space of a couple of days. Such a minute quantity. And if the Honourable Chamber would like to know, I would like to tell you what steps I took later on in order to obtain oxygen.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And finally --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. That would be 2703. And finally, Your Honour, on this topic, I would like -- this is not an article that -- it's another article from Vreme from the internet dated June the 29th. And if that could be...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, it's only in English, Mr. Radic. But Vreme, do you recall, published an article at the end of June 1992 on the topic of the Banja Luka babies?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember because we didn't read Vreme.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And the suggestion from Vreme who set out the history of this was this was propaganda being put out by the Bosnian Serbs. Were you aware of that, Mr. Radic?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is really a disgrace, Madam Prosecutor, a sheer disgrace. I will bring a book and put it at the disposal of the Honourable Chamber. The book was written by a pediatric surgeon and lists the names and the dates of all the things that happened. This is nothing but a pamphlet written by this Mr. Milos Vasic. This is just propaganda, it's a disgrace, Madam Prosecutor. And it is real disgraceful, to contrast a document of this nature to the 12 babies that died. There are witnesses to that. There are international institutions that registered those deaths. And what you can read in Vreme is a sheer disgrace, nothing but a disgrace.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could that be made P2704, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could I deal with one other matter in connection with what you said about the SOS before we look at what you said in interview, and that was in connection with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Ms. Korner. Yes, Mr. Radic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what your rules are in this courtroom and whether I can deliver a book to you via the Defence counsels, a book that documents the events involving the 12 babies which show that this was no Serbian propaganda. This book deals with over 12 babies who died.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I authorise you to do so, provided Mr. Ackerman accepts to hand it over.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of course, I wouldn't imagine there would be.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, you dealt with the Banja Luka Corps. You were asked about one of the demands, that is, the breaks up of the Banja Luka corps. And you were asked this: "Did this crisis staff that was created - that is your crisis staff - have any competency to issue orders to the supreme command or the presidency of Yugoslavia?" And you said "No, not at all." This is page 16 of the LiveNote. "The municipal assembly of Banja Luka couldn't do this, not even the National Assembly of Republika Srpska. An order arrived from the main staff of the JNA requesting all officers withdraw by the 15th of May and be transferred to Yugoslavia. Most of them obeyed this order and returned to Yugoslavia. But some of them remained there. I would like to tell you that that was the smallest corps in the JNA and it consisted of about 1.500 men. I am talking about the Banja Luka Corps." Do you want to stand by that answer, Mr. Radic?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Would you like, please, to have a look first of all at P6. No, P2417. Part of it, I'm sorry. And if you give it to me, I will find the... Could I have the English first, please. All right. Could we have the English on the ELMO, page 79.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I take Mr. Ackerman's point actually -- here we are. Got it. All right. Well, at the moment -- Your Honour, I'm having some difficulty finding this in the B/C/S. The English -- I've got it, I think. Found it. Thank you. That page, please, to be shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is a report of the 2nd military district command, 23rd of January 1992. It includes a list of the manning levels of the corps within that command. Do you see the 5th Corps total manning level? 17.539 people.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Slowly, slowly. Wartime. Peacetime. 2.815. I would like you to --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you go to the last column, please, Mr. Radic. Under "total manning level."

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The last column, I can see 17.753 [as interpreted]. Yes, this is the column here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Sorry, stop, Mr. Radic. 17.539. Not 1.753.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because the second part of this number is not legible on my copy because -- but I would really like you to ask this question of a military expert, not me, because I was told that this was the smallest corps on the strength of the Yugoslav People's Army, and that's a fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So what you're saying is you didn't know one way or the other when you asserted that it was the smallest corps consisting of only 1.500 people?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Regular troops. Regular troops.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I'm going to suggest to you by the 23rd of May, Mr. Radic, the size of the corps had risen to some 40.000 men and officers. I'm sorry, more than that, in fact.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam Prosecutor, I'm talking about the regular army which were there. And those people that you are talking about were mobilised. And again, I kindly ask you to invite experts. I believe that some will be invited as witnesses. They will be able to tell you about the strength of the 5th Corps on the eve of the war. I'm not an expert for that. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. However, according to the information that I received from them, this was the smallest corps in the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What makes you believe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: 66, line 4. It's minor. But what he said was: "The last column, I see 1.753." I think it's clear from the next question of Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I see it. We can leave it as it is, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What leads you to believe, Mr. Radic, that a military expert is going to be called?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because it would be appropriate for a military expert to witness the strength of the army. I really can't be a witness to that. I don't know who reserves are. I don't know who active army is. There are younger officers, 190-something, and so on and so forth. But these are just my assumption. I cannot be the best interpreter of what the -- what it says here and when they told me, the military experts told me that this was the smallest corps of the Yugoslav People's Army, I believed them. It was some sort of a reserve or an auxiliary corps as far as I understood it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. When did you ask an expert how many people were in the 5th/1st Krajina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: He didn't say he asked an expert, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "The military experts told me..."

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: He didn't say he asked.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was just told to us.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Experts told us that this was the smallest corps. And this sticks in my mind, and you should really ask these experts how big the corps really was and what was its strength in Banja Luka. Now, if you insist on who told me and when they told me, I don't know. This was just something that was a figure -- a figure being given to us on the eve of the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I'm just going to ask you this again: You've told us a moment ago that you believe that military -- I've lost it now -- now. "I believe that some" -- you said: "I kindly ask you to invite experts. I believe that some will be invited as witnesses." Why do you believe that some will be invited as witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: She asked that, and it was answered. He said he just made that assumption because they're military issues here. I think he said something like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we should leave it and proceed, Ms. Korner. You're not going to get anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. I thought I was getting somewhere. Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's have a break. 20 minutes from now, resuming at 10 minutes to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, I'm going to ask you to look at a couple of excerpts from the interview you gave to us. I'd like you to first look at page 65 in the B/C/S, and page 64 in the English of the first interview in 2001. 64 in English; 65 in B/C/S. Do you see there, Mr. Radic, you were asked at the top of the page, you can see, about the arrival of the SOS? You were if you recall that, and you said: "Of course, I do." It was put to you there was negotiation held with the SOS about certain demands that they had. And you said there that the only demand they had was to be allowed to stay in town and continue doing what they were doing. However, Mr. Radic, it's right to say you hadn't seen the documents at that stage, so I'm not suggesting there that you were trying to mislead. But I want to know about the bottom part. It was put to you: "So you're saying there was nothing you could have done about the existence of the SOS which is a paramilitary organisation in Banja Luka?" "Something probably could have been done, but it would have been partial. They could not have been eliminated entirely without strong police and military forces, and I've also wanted to know who actually manipulated them." "What made you think they were manipulated?" You said: "Because despite police and military measures, they would remain here. We knew exactly who they were. They would sometimes -- they would just disappear and go to Belgrade and come back later." "Who do you think that they were working for, war profiteers? And who would those be in Banja Luka that allowed them to stay? "No one could allow them. They didn't ask anyone." "But they must have had protectors who they paid." Question: "At high levels?" "Whether we are talking about high levels or people with a lot of money, I don't know." Do you still stick by that answer, or answers?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Then, I'd like you to have a look, please, at the second interview now - you can hand that back to the usher - where the question of the SOS was gone over again. And could you look, please, first of all at page 39 in the English, which is -- I think it's 39, yes. Which is 36 and 37 in the Serbian language. All right. We don't, apparently --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could I have -- is that the first interview in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. You have been given the page already, have you? Can I just put this into context for you, Mr. Radic. You had been shown earlier a document compiled by the General Tolimir who was the top security person in the RS where it said that Nenad Stevandic was the leader of the SOS.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And Your Honours, that's already exhibited in our case as P400.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you were asked: "Do you agree with that, that Colonel Tolimir wrote about the SOS?" And you said: "I do, yes, because I have no reason not to trust Tolimir, who's a top security guy." And then the investigator dealt with the Stevandic part, and the investigator put to you a long question to the effect that the arrival of the SOS and the demands were a ploy. Effectively what I've been putting to you. And your response: "The way you put it, their appearance must have been orchestrated from somewhere." And you were asked who. And you said: "Yes, because the SOS couldn't appoint themselves" --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, although it says "they" in the English transcript, I gather in the B/C/S it says SOS, and I think we can see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- "somebody had to prepare the territory, and the appearance of the SOS, there's a strange coincidence between that and the decision we received from Pale to form the crisis staff." And then you explained about the decision. And then at the bottom of the page, the article was read to you: "`At a press conference today, Predrag Radic, president of the Banja Luka Crisis Staff, declared that all SOS demands had been agreed to.'" . "True, in a slightly modified way." "Is that true or false?" And your answer is this, and this is page 41: "Of course it is yes. It is obvious" --

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a minute. I can't follow.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're going too fast. 41, I don't have that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Page 38 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 38, I see.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And your answer to that, at the top of the page: "Of course it is, yes, because it was obvious, and I couldn't reject anything because I knew, I realised that there was -- they were being dictated from somewhere." And then it was put to you you agreed to all their demands, and you said you didn't say you agreed to all their demands. And it was put to you again, you said earlier to Mr. Grady that you didn't know where the SOS were getting their instructions from or why they were at this meeting with you, but you're saying you agreed in modified form to their demands. Answer: "Because a good portion of it fits in with what we received from Pale." "So in essence, a good portion of what the SOS was asking for was what the SDS in Pale was asking for. Correct?" And you say: "It wasn't the SDS, it was the president of the government and the president of the republic. And there is a list of what the crisis staff should do." And do you still stick by those answers, Mr. Radic?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, they must have received instructions from a very high level, so that was acceptable.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then finally on this point, and then we'll leave the SOS, it was -- you were asked: "Who were the president in the presidency and the government that were making the decisions?" And you said: "It's very well known who was in the presidency." Question: "Yeah. Who?" And then you answered: "Ms. Plavsic - it was a collective body of the presidency - Ms. Plavsic, Mr. Koljevic, Mr. Krajisnik, Mr. Karadzic. So it was a collective body. How can I say it was Mr. Karadzic"? That's effectively what you said to us yesterday. And finally, the question: "Fine. So what we're saying is that the demands of the SOS in Banja Luka broadly corresponded with the demands that you had been instructed to implement by Biljana Plavsic, Krajisnik, and Karadzic from Pale?" Answer, from you: "Yeah, the four member of the presidency in Pale." "So the answer to the question is yes?" And you said: "It came to me as a paper, as a document, and I had to implement it. And it's a fact. You'll find the same piece of paper in Trebinje, in Prijedor, wherever they sent it." Question: "And that is why publicly you agreed in modified form to the demands of the SOS?" Your answer: "I'm not going to say yes. I'm not going to say yes because what the demands I received had to be modified in order to be implemented because the modification was done in accordance with to the order I received from" -- and there was an interruption -- "Pale." And again, do you stick by those answers?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because we all received such instructions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. That's all I want to ask you about the SOS. And I want to move, please, I hope fairly quickly now, through some of the other documents. Can you look, now, please at a document, P1617. I'm sorry. I've made a mistake. I'm sorry. It's my fault. It's not going to be a transcript. I've made a note of a wrong exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. Ms. Gustin will turn it up very quickly. I see, it is an attachment to that. If you give me the whole exhibit, please, 1617, and I'll just extract the right one. It's just the documents I want, and I'll just pick out the right one for you. Your Honour, this is P1617/S124.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is from Stakic, no?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. It doesn't appear to be in this. It should be, but it isn't. Yes. Thank you. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, can you have a look, please, at this document. And we'll put the English on the ELMO. Do you remember a gentleman called Barney Mayhew from ECMM?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is a report that he prepared on the -- of a meeting with you on the 13th of April 1992. And you explain to him your view of the Serbian Republic within Bosnia and Herzegovina. And you told him, according to Mr. Mayhew's report, that he -- that you expected to be appointed at the vice-president. Did you expect that in April?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That I told him that I was be the vice-president? Of what? Of the republic?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you expect that you would be appointed a vice-president of the Serbian Republic in April of 1992?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Did you ever say that to Mr. Mayhew?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. How could I have been the vice-president of the republic? What next?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Then you explained that there would be five parts to the Serbian Republic within Bosnia and Herzegovina, according to Mr. Mayhew. In fact, you set out the five autonomous regions. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Usher, could we have the correct part on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that was what was discussed, the existence of these five --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Autonomous regions.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you explain to him that in your view the capital would be Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was natural for Banja Luka to be the capital.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. All I'm asking you, Mr. Radic, is did you tell Mr. Mayhew that?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The assumption that Banja Luka would be the capital, that's something that was constantly present. I told him that that was a possibility. When you put it this way, well, yes, I certainly said that Banja Luka is the town that should be the capital.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Then, the next -- paragraph 4, Once the Muslim and Croat constituent units of BiH are established, you foresaw a small central government responsible for certain aspects of fiscal policy and foreign policy. But saying "once the Muslim and Croat constituent units of BiH were established," were you saying that there would be separate Serb, separate Muslim, and separate Croat?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, that had almost been an agreement, so I didn't tell him anything new.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Do you remember him asking you whether it was the plebiscite that had taken place in November which gave the authority for the Serbian Republic, and your reply, that the republic was a result of the wishes of the Serbian people?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. And that was confirmed in the plebiscite.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. In paragraph 6, you were asked about the statement of principles in Brussels. Paragraph 7 has been chopped off in my copy. Paragraph 8, you apparently said that in your view, the European Community strongly favoured Croatia and Slovenia. Did you express such views to him?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not what it says on this item 6 here. It says that I said --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, 8. Sorry, 8?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Eight, oh, I see. I thought it was six. Yes, well it was obvious that at the time Croatia and Slovenia had already been declared as states, so the fact that they were in favour of them, that they supported them, is not a secret at all. But that they conducted a campaign against the orthodox church, I don't think I -- but if the person says that that is what I said.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. But then he remarks that you were friendly towards him. And finally this: "The Livno/Duvno situation. Mr. Radic warned that we should not be surprised if we took Croatian civilian hostages in order to exchange them for Serb civilian hostages held in Rascani near Duvno. We warn him that the EC would view this with great concern, and that he would lose any moral advantage that he now has. We promised him that ECMM teams would do what they could to help any Serb hostages and urged him to be patient." Did you threaten or did you tell him that you might take Croatian civilian hostages?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it says if he takes Croatian civilians as hostages. How would I do that? I said that it was a possibility that Croatians might be taken as hostages to have an exchange in Rascani. Mr. Mihijun [phoen], Mr. Botonakis went to Rascani, that was the result, and they saw what they saw there. A month or two later, the Serbs from Rascani were released. These are people from Tomislavgrad who had been confined in the village of Rascani.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I understand that, Mr. Radic. What I'm asking you is were you saying at this stage that Croats presumably in Banja Luka would be held as hostages for exchange with the Serbian hostages in Rascani?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember having expressed it in that way, that I would -- rather, that he would have hostages who would be exchanged for those people. I didn't even know how many of them there were in Rascani, but I drew his attention to the fact that it was time to go there and to see for themselves. In any case, it says Botonakis and Majir [phoen] here. We went there together. This should be understood. And a month later, these people were released without any hostages, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. That's all I'm going to ask you about that document. Can you look, please, just very briefly, please, at Glas for the 21st of April, which is P157. I'm sorry, 154. I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Has he been given 154?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is in connection with what you said about the dismissals. This is Glas 21st April, conversation with Mr. Brdjanin, dismissals according to the wishes of the people. And there you see in the beginning part of the article the basic reason for the conversation of Radoslav Brdjanin, the vice-president, et cetera, charged with putting through the demands already accepted of the Serbian Defence forces about personnel changes. And there you can see, Mr. Radic, I suggest to you Mr. Brdjanin explaining what steps are being taken. And can you find the part where Mr. Brdjanin mentions, he mentions a number of names. Talks about Merkur, a firm called Konzum company, and then Metal, Mr. Osmancevic. In fact, Mr. Brdjanin asserting that the managing board of this firm must urgently hold session and meet the demands of the Serbian Defence Forces and of this commission and from the point of view of personnel levelling relieve Dzevad Osmancevic director of the company and Ecim Skor [phoen] sales director. And so on and so forth. So do you accept, Mr. Radic, having been reminded of that article that the implementation began very, very shortly after the SOS made those demands?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the date shows that it's the 21st of April, and that was on the 3rd of April. 18 days later. But it here it says this was an implementation of the request made by the crisis staff. And the -- on taking over the SOS, taking over by the SOS. So yes, later, there were dismissals. But you can see that Boro Vitkovic who was a Serb was also replaced in the service centre which also didn't satisfy certain demands. So yes, they were replaced.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The way it was put earlier was that Serbs who hadn't voted in favour of the Serbian State were also liable to dismissal. And that was right, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a little more difficult to determine, to determine who hadn't voted in the plebiscite for remaining within Yugoslavia. But that was also put. You don't want to remain in Yugoslavia, so you cannot continue in your role as managers. That was also a request.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, again, briefly, because you've looked at this document before, and identified it. Can you be shown P157. Those are the instructions from the prime minister, Mr. Dzeric. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is right. 26 April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It sets out what needs to be done in respect of the work of the municipal crisis staffs. And in the last paragraph, 14: "The crisis staff shall convene and make decisions in the presence of all its members, take official minutes, issue written decisions, and submit weekly reports to the regional and state organisations of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina." In the case of the Krajina, the regional organisation was the assembly, and then the crisis staff. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Will you please repeat this. You are talking about item 14, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Item 14: "The municipal crisis staff" -- it says "the crisis staff" but the directions are to the municipal. "Shall convene and make decisions in the presence of all its members," et cetera, "and submit weekly reports to the regional and state organisations." I'm not asking if you submitted weekly reports, Mr. Radic. All I'm asking you is to confirm that in the Autonomous Region of Krajina, the regional organisation was the autonomous region assembly; and when that didn't meet, the autonomous region crisis staff.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the assembly existed and worked. The crisis staff was established and also worked. That is, the crisis staff of the AR Krajina. So both bodies worked.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because here, there's no mention of the regional -- that is, of the regions which later on became. This is what Mr. Dzeric wrote 22 days after the beginning of the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. In reality, it's right, isn't it, it was only the Autonomous Region of Krajina that ever had a proper functioning, working assembly?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were others, for example, SAO Romanija, SAO Herzegovina, they also had their respective assemblies. Not only the AR Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: Did you know Mr. Perisic, the head of the -- the president of the northern autonomous region? The Autonomous Region of North Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you never see Mr. Perisic at the meetings of the assembly or at the crisis staff, the regional crisis staff, from Teslic?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He is not from the northern part. He is from Teslic, indeed. And I knew him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But that is not the north of the country.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. All right. Was he not -- well, did you know -- if you don't, say so. Did you know that he was supposedly president of the Autonomous Region of Northern Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. How could he be the president of the region of Northern Bosnia if he was from Teslic? In the north, you have Posavina, Semberija, and that is in the north. So he could not be the president of the northern part of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In fact, in the document we just looked at, the Serb Autonomous District of North Bosnia was meant to include Doboj, and Teslic, Semberija, Bijeljina, and other places. Do you remember that? If you don't, say so. I don't want to waste time on it.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't remember. Nothing indicated -- there was no indication that this could be the case in that region.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: One final document, and I think that will then deal with it for today. Would you please look at P278. Again, this is an article in Glas much later, on the 10th of July, where the Autonomous Region of Krajina Crisis Staff changed its name to War Presidency. It was -- Brdjanin gave an explanation saying: "The establishment of the AR Krajina Crisis Staff or the municipal crisis staff is no invention of ours. The Government of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina passed the decision to form them, and Dr. Branko Dzeric signed it, abolishing the crisis staff," Brdjanin went on to say, "has caused some ambiguity and doubt about the previous decisions of our crisis staff having any legal weight. This is incorrect because essentially the war presidency is carrying on the same work as did the crisis staff, which means that all our previously passed crisis staff decisions will have to be carried out." And so on and so forth. Just two questions: Was it about this time also that the Banja Luka Municipal Crisis Staff became known as the war presidency?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to answer that question, whether the municipal staff became war presidency. I would have to consult documents. I cannot answer this question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a very short document. Speaks about Atlas, about Putnik, the return of weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It was just that part that I want to deal with. And finally for today, Mr. Radic, were you present at the assembly on the 17th of July, the assembly of the autonomous region, when all the decisions taken by the regional crisis staff of the ARK were verified?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's all for today. I thank you once more, Mr. Radic. You'll be escorted by Mr. Usher, and we'll see you again tomorrow afternoon, 2.15.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could I ask Your Honour to remain behind after Mr. Radic has left Court. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I also had recognised Mr. Ackerman standing up.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I was just wondering if there's any chance at all that we can meet in the morning rather than the afternoon. I know you'd looked into that. But I noticed that the Nikolic case is over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I have a meeting with the other two Judges in the other case I was sitting in on this morning. And that's at 10.00. And I don't know how long it's going to last. Then I have another meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I say, because I checked to make sure when we were sitting, I do have meetings now organised involving the Prosecutor and effectively all the STAs tomorrow morning at 11.00 on the basis that we'd be sitting in the afternoon. To reorganise would really cause all sorts of problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because I had already agreed with Judge Mumba and Judge Schomburg -- I had agreed that we would sit immediately in conference --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No problem, Your Honour. Tomorrow afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the only query I have is whether Your Honour is going to put a time limit on me now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think, Ms. Korner, let's put it like this: If you could avoid me having to do that, that would be better.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If I can take the whole day tomorrow, I've got ample material to fill the whole of tomorrow. If Your Honour tells me I can't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's do this. I must first confer with Judge Taya and Judge Janu to see whether there are any questions. And also, the re-examination, redirect.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I agree, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which I suppose there will be, having observed things. So let's talk about it tomorrow. In the meantime, perhaps, Mr. Ackerman --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, to make it clear, I need to know in advance of tomorrow's sitting because I need to know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: My intention is to have the testimony of this witness concluded tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, can I last how long Your Honour is giving me, then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know how long Mr. Ackerman requires in redirect. That's more important than how much we require.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: He won't know until I finish cross. That's the problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I know. But at least based on what we have covered today, he probably has an idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Right now, I would say around a half an hour. Maybe a little more. And after what happens tomorrow, it may be a little more. I really can't say for sure right now.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I explain the difficulty. It's this: Clearly from any point of view -- as I've said already, from the Defence point of view, this is a big witness. From your point of view, I don't know. But you may think that hearing Mr. Radic is important. He's said many, many things in his evidence in chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Definitely, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Which, Your Honour, I would wish to demonstrate, putting it at its lowest, an error. Otherwise, if I don't have the opportunity to do that, then it stays, and Mr. Ackerman is entitled to rely on it in his final address. And that's the real difficulty. Your Honour, if we can start earlier, perhaps, tomorrow. And the trouble is I can see Mr. Radic gets tired. I mean, I agree with Your Honour on that, what the difficulty is. But if we can start earlier, perhaps having proper breaks, then I will conclude tomorrow in time for Mr. Ackerman. But not if we're just sitting again from 2.15 to 6.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, a great deal of this time has been taken up by the Prosecution not able to show Mr. Radic where things are. Plus, Your Honour, when we were cross-examining Prosecution witnesses, you told Mr. Cunningham and Madam Baruch one day that there's no way in the world that a cross-examination should be permitted to exceed the length of a direct examination. I think I can find your words in the transcript to that effect. She has now been going on and on and on, and a lot of it just completely useless time-wasting as far as I'm concerned. But certainly useless time-wasting with regard to not being properly prepared. And now to say she wants to keep Mr. Radic here over the weekend because she did not get properly prepared to cross-examine him, I think is just -- I think she's had enough time. I think she should end fairly early tomorrow and let him go home. Just have her structure her cross-examination to finish tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll take a decision tomorrow after discussing amongst ourselves, but be prepared to finish tomorrow. And roughly, we're saying, because then everyone has to make a sacrifice, or sacrifice something, I would say knock off maximum of three-quarters of an hour from the day, if necessary. I think it will not be fair on the witness to start in the morning, and then have a break, and then bring him here again. He was dead tired today. So we'll try and finish tomorrow. We've had -- he has been here since Monday? Since Monday. And he took -- your direct was a day and a half?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: About a day and a half, Your Honour. I finished sort of middle of the session, I think, on Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we've had the whole of Wednesday, the whole of Thursday, and part of Tuesday. I think you need to finish tomorrow, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: As I say, I mean, I merely pointed out what I consider to be the importance of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, okay. But stick yourself to the important questions. I recognise there is quite some territory to be covered on the events that took place in Banja Luka. But I put pressure on the witness as well tomorrow, and we conclude.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, regardless of what Mr. Ackerman may say about the preparedness of the Prosecution, perhaps --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Forget that. I don't think I can agree or accept that you are not prepared.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I finish. I'm merely going to invite Your Honour to ask Mr. Radic again to answer, if it's a question that can be answered yes or no, to answer it yes or no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Tomorrow I will control him to the best of my ability, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I wish to thank the interpreters and the technicians and the rest of the staff. We have overstayed by about 7 minutes. I thank you. And we'll all meet tomorrow at 2.15. If we can find a better courtroom tomorrow, change this one. I think it will be better, rather than stay, because it's almost claustrophobic, this one. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 7th day of November, 2003, at 2.15 p.m. 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 6.37 p.m.,
